explanation: The corneal topography shown above shows a region of marked steepening in the inferior cornea consistent with the diagnosis of keratoconus (about 54 diopters in the region of greatest steepening and about 44 diopters centrally). While other entities can cause irregular astigmatism including contact lens use, these findings are more than would be expected for contact lens associated topography changes and the patient has not worn his contacts for at least one month according to the question stem. question: A 34-year-old man undergoes a deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) for keratoconus. His post-operative drop regimen consists only of topical corticosteroids and antibiotics. On his post-operative week two visit, the patient complains of photophobia and glare. On exam, you note a fixed dilated pupil and some sector iris atrophy. What is the name given to these clinical findings?
explanation: The presentation of a fixed dilated pupil with sector iris atrophy after penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) is classically known as Urrets-Zavalia syndrome. It was originally described in 1963 as a rare complication in keratoconus patients who underwent PKP. The original description also included secondary glaucoma as part of the syndrome (although this was rarely reported in later cases). Since then, it has been described in cases of deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK), trabeculectomy, and even after argon laser iridoplasty. The cause of this syndrome is not completely understood, but is thought to be a result of parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter. Answer choices "B" and "D" are made-up; Answer choice "A" is a classic glaucoma syndrome characterized by recurrent, unilateral bouts of very-high IOPs. These episodes are self-limited and associated with only very mild anterior chamber inflammation.

question: Which of the following conditions is associated with keratoglobus?
explanation: Keratoglobus differs from the other corneal ectatic disorders (e.g. from keratoconus and pellucid) in that it is typically present at birth. Unlike keratoconus or pellucid, keratoglobus is frequently associated with corneal perforation and rupture. Keratoglobus shows strong association with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type VI and blue sclera. It is also associated with flexible joints, bone fractures, deafness, and teeth abnormalities. An increased risk of keratoconus (not keratoglobus) occurs in patients with atopy, Marfan syndrome, floppy eyelid syndrome, and mitral valve prolapse. The classic clinical vignette for a patient with keratoconus is a young adult who has a history of chronic eye rubbing during childhood. Some other conditions commonly in the differential diagnosis of keratoglobus are megalocornea and congenital glaucoma. Unlike keratoglobus, the corneal thickness and contour are normal in megalocornea (defined as horizontal cornea diameter ≥13 mm). In congenital glaucoma, there may be corneal edema and Haab's striae which do not occur in keratoglobus.

question: Which of the following best distinguishes keratoglobus from pellucid marginal degeneration and keratoconus?
explanation: Keratoglobus is a very rare corneal ectasia which features a globular overall corneal curvature. The pattern of thinning with keratoglobus is generalized thinning, greatest in the periphery. Keratoconus generally thins paracentrally, and pellucid has a normal thickness peripherally with thinning in a band centripetal to this. Also in contrast to keratoconus or pellucid, keratoglobus is typically present at birth while the other two corneal ectasias occur in puberty or young adulthood. Keratoconus, the most common of the corneal ectasias, is a degenerative disorder that results in thinning of the cornea at the apex of the cone. These patients almost always demonstrate topographic abnormalities at a young age. It is thought to develop initially in puberty. It is commonly associated with painful episodes of corneal hydrops, apical scarring, and "Fleischer rings" below the cone. Pellucid marginal degeneration has inferior thinning of the cornea with protrusion of the cornea above the thinning (i.e. the corneal apex is above the area of thinning). Corneal scarring, episodes of hydrops, and iron lines are less common in pellucid compared to keratoconus. In clinical practice, it is sometimes very difficult to distinguish between pellucid and keratoconus. Differentiating between these entities can be accomplished by obtaining pachymetry measurements and correlating it to the topography. This task is easier to do with devices such as Scheimpflug cameras (e.g. Pentacam) which are able to produce topographic and pachymetry data simultaneously. Answer choice C is incorrect because both pellucid and keratoglobus have peripheral thinning. In addition, answer choice A is the most correct answer and a topic that is readily testable on the boards.

explanation: llucid marginal degeneration (PMD) is a bilateral and peripheral corneal ectatic disorder which is characterized by a band of thinning typically in the inferior cornea (e.g. 4 o'clock to 8 o'clock). The maximal protrusion in PMD occurs just superior to the area of thinning. This contrasts with keratoconus where the maximal protrusion typically coincides with the area of maximal thinning. The protruding portion of the cornea in PMD is of normal thickness. Thus, the ectatic pattern of PMD is sometimes referred to as a "beer belly" (i.e. someone's gut [the protruding area] hanging over his belt [the thin area] ). The topographic pattern of PMD is classically described as "crab claw" (i.e. central flattening with inferior steepening). The classic differences between pellucid, keratoconus, and keratoglobus are: Keratoconus • more common • usually starts at puberty • maximal thinning at the apex • Fleischer ring • Scarring is common Pellucid marginal degeneration • less common • onset during 20's-40's • maximal thinning inferior to area of protrusion • Scarring only occurs after hydrops Keratoglobus • very rare • onset at birth • thinning greatest in periphery • protrusion is generalized • No iron lines or scarring Corneal scarring, episodes of hydrops, and iron lines are less common in pellucid compared to keratoconus. In clinical practice, it is sometimes very difficult to distinguish between pellucid and keratoconus. Differentiating between these entities can be accomplished by obtaining pachymetry measurements and correlating it to the topography. This task is easier to do with devices such as Scheimpflug cameras (e.g. Pentacam) which are able to produce topographic and pachymetry data simultaneously.

question: What is the classic topographic finding in patients with pellucid marginal degeneration (PMD)?
explanation: Pellucid marginal degeneration (PMD) is a bilateral ectatic disorder that features a band of thinning, approximately 1-2 mm in width, in the inferior cornea (e.g. from 4 o'clock to 8 o'clock). Protrusion of the cornea is seen above this area of thinning, which is in contrast to keratoconus where the protrusion is within the area of thinning. Corneal scarring, episodes of hydrops, and iron lines are less common in PMD compared to keratoconus. In clinical practice, it is sometimes very difficult to distinguish between pellucid and keratoconus. Differentiating between these entities can be accomplished by obtaining pachymetry measurements and correlating it to the topography. Keratoconus has thinning directly over the area of maximal protrusion. This task is easier to do with devices such as Scheimpflug cameras (e.g. Pentacam) which are able to produce topographic and pachymetry data simultaneously. The classic topographic pattern for PMD is the "crab claw" configuration (see image below) which represents the shift from against-the-rule astigmatism superiorly to with-the-rule astigmatism inferiorly. The classic topographic pattern for keratoconus is the inferior steepening or asymmetric bowtie pattern.

options.C: Intraocular lens calculations may be inaccurate in this patient population
options.D: Light microscopy will reveal a focal absence of endothelium and Descemet's membrane with secondary opacification of overlying stromal lamellae

explanation: The clinical findings seen in this patient are consistent with posterior keratoconus, which is thought to be a developmental disorder that occurs during the second trimester. This condition causes a localized anterior bulging of the posterior corneal surface with overlying thinning of stroma, similar in appearance to a corneal leukoma. This condition is in the spectrum of anterior chamber dysgenesis syndromes and there may be other anterior segment abnormalities present, though many cases are isolated findings with minimal-to-moderate visual impairment. Light microscopy of this condition has shown a focal disorganization of basal epithelium and basement membrane, replacement of Bowman's membrane by fibrous tissue, and a thinned stroma with irregular arrangement of central collagen fibers. There is a variable appearance of Descemet's membrane with posterior indentations. If unilateral, trauma (oblique, blunt injury) and perforated corneal ulcer may be considered. However, most cases are bilateral, and therefore the differential includes conditions such as Peter's anomaly and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy. Genetic testing may be considered though no specific genetic defects have been identified thus far. This condition may be associated with other anterior segment pathology, such as polar cataract, lenticonus and ectopia lentis. Interestingly enough, there is minimal-to-no association with traditional keratoconus. Corneal thickness may be significantly thinner in the area of the lesion as compared to the rest of the cornea. The refractive power of the cornea also may be dramatically different, and thus intraocular lens (IOL) calculations may be especially challenging in these patients. Intraoperative aberrometry may help IOL calculations, but preoperative discussion should be made with these patients regarding challenges of accurate IOL selection, and the potential need for glasses/contact lenses even after uneventful cataract surgery. Treatment for this condition includes maximizing vision potential with glasses/contact lenses, especially in the pediatric population, to minimize the risk of amblyopia. Posterior KCN rarely becomes severe enough to require surgical intervention, but if needed, a penetrating keratoplasty (not endothelial keratoplasty) would be the surgical procedure of choice.

question: Which of the following is seen with Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy (LECD)?

options.B: the cornea is clear between the bands of cysts
options.C: it is often associated with recurrent erosions
options.D: cysts covering the visual axis may require an anterior lamellar keratoplasty

explanation: Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy (LECD) is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion. It is characterized by densely-crowded epithelial microcysts that occur in a "band-like" or "feathery" pattern. Between the bands, the corneal epithelium is clear. Generally, treatment is not needed unless a band crosses the visual axis in which case the epithelium can be scraped. These patients typically do not have epithelial erosions. Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy most closely resembles Meesmann corneal dystrophy. Lisch and Meesmann both have intraepithelial microcysts. The difference between these two dystrophies is that Meesmann has diffuse, evenly- spaced cysts while Lisch has broad, band-shaped, feathery lesions in whorled patterns that are more densely crowded together. explanation: The slit-lamp photograph shows multiple, small epithelial vesicles or microcysts. This corneal finding is characteristic of Meesmann corneal dystrophy, which is an autosomal dominant disease which typically affects individuals early in life. These microcysts consist of degenerated epithelial cell products that are PAS-positive and also contain an electron-dense accumulation of granular/filamentary material called "peculiar substance" (hint: buzzword). These microcysts are most numerous in the interpalpebral area and extend out to the limbus. Corneal sensation may be reduced and some mild corneal thinning may occur. Typically, patients only experience mild foreign body sensation, but occasionally painful recurrent erosions can occur (but not nearly as frequent as in the stromal dystrophies). Visual acuity is only mildly reduced in these patients. The causative mutation occurs in the keratin K3 (KRT3) or the keratin K12 (KRT12) ("Stocker- Holt variant") genes. Most patients with Meesmann require no treatment besides artificial tears and occasionally contact lens wear for frequent symptoms. Very rarely, superficial PTK is used to reduce symptoms. Another helpful hint: these microcysts can be seen best in retroillumination. Thus, if the exam shows you a corneal photograph in retroillumination, then Meesman is the likely condition in question. Lastly, another name for Meesman is juvenile hereditary epithelial dystrophy.

question: Central Cloudy Dystrophy of Francois is characterized by diamond shaped opacities with clear intervening spaces. What degeneration is identical in appearance to Central Cloudy Dystrophy of Francois?

Although there have been familial cases that suggest an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, most cases are not familial suggesting a sporadic or degenerative disorder. This disorder is characterized by bilateral, symmetric, polygonal, cloudy gray stromal opacities separated by relatively clear zones in the central cornea. Patients usually present with asymmetric, nonprogress bilateral corneal opacities that is not visually significant.[1] Treatment is usually not indicated for CCDF.

question: What is the inheritance pattern of the corneal dystrophy seen in the photo above?
explanation: Lattice corneal dystrophy (LCD) of the cornea features glasslike branching lines in the stroma. Recent genetic classification of lattice dystrophies sort them into the classic type 1 (LCD1) versus other "variants" which include types IIIA, I/IIIA, IV, and polymorphic amyloidosis. This autosomal dominant corneal dystrophy is caused by a mutation in locus 5q31 containing the gene TGFBI. The abnormal gene leads to improper protein folding with subsequent amyloid accumulation in tissues. The "variants" are also due to a defect in the gene TGFBI and are inherited autosomal dominantly but present later in life compared to the classic type 1. The eponymous term Meretoja syndrome or lattice corneal dystrophy type II should be referred to as familial amyloidosis, Finnish type, or gelsolin type. It is due to a mutation in a totally different gene (9q32-34 or the gelsolin gene) and has corneal lattice-like changes with systemic amyloidosis. It is no longer considered a dystrophy. Lattice corneal dystrophy is basically primary localized corneal amyloidosis. In LCD1, deposits start in the anterior cornea (subepithelial and anterior stroma) and then progress posteriorly. They also start centrally and progress centrifugally. LCD type IIIA has recurrent erosions that start later in life. LCD type IV has more posteriorly located corneal deposits and is unlikely to present with recurrent erosions. In addition to staining with Congo red, it demonstrates "metachromasia" if stained with crystal violet. These amyloid deposits will also appear apple-green in color when viewed under polarized light, a property known as "birefringence." These deposits will also display the property of "dichroism" where the deposits alternate in color from red to green when viewed through a rotating polarizing filter. Of the stromal dystrophies, lattice has the highest rate of recurrence in corneal transplant patients followed by granular and then macular dystrophies. question: What is the inheritance pattern of Fleck corneal dystrophy?
explanation: Fleck dystrophy is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is characterized by dandruff-like deposits throughout the stroma but sparing the epithelium, Bowman layer, Descemet's membrane, and endothelium. Vision is not usually decreased in this condition and it is non-progressive and can be highly-asymmetric or even unilateral. Extra: all corneal dystrophies have autosomal dominant inheritance except for Macular, CHED 2 (nystagmus associated), and gelatinous.

question: Which of the following corneal dystrophies is the LEAST common in North America?
explanation: f these choices, Fuchs corneal dystrophy is by far the most common corneal dystrophy followed by lattice, granular, and finally macular dystrophy. Of the three classic stromal dystrophies, macular dystrophy is also the most severe in terms of vision loss. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by mutations in the CHST6 gene (carbohydrate sulfotransferase) on chromosome 16. The symmetric corneal changes of this dystrophy are typically first noticed in the adolescent years as a diffuse, fine, superficial clouding in the central stroma. By the 2nd decade of life, this cloudiness extends to the periphery and typically involves the full thickness of the cornea. The Descemet's membrane may take on a guttate appearance. Macular corneal dystrophy can be associated with severe photophobia and recurrent erosions. There are 3 immunotypes of this dystrophy based on the reactivity of the individual's serum and corneal tissue to an antibody that recognizes sulfated keratan sulfate: • type I: no detectable antigenic keratan sulfate • type IA: serum lacks antigenic keratan sulfate but the keratocytes have antigenic keratan sulfate • type II: normal amounts of antigenic keratan sulfate Histopathologically, macular corneal dystrophy is characterized by the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) between the stromal lamellae, within the keratocytes and endothelial cells, and underneath the epithelium. These GAGs classically stain with Alcian blue (the mnemonic: "Maryilyn Monroe Always...") but also stain with colloidal iron, Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS), and metachromatic dyes. explanation: The concepts of imbibition pressure (IP) and swelling pressure (SP) are often confusing to students and therefore a review these concepts may be helpful (Figure 1). Normally, the stroma contains negatively-charged glycosaminoglycans (GAGs, mainly dermatan sulfate in the anterior cornea and keratan sulfate in the posterior cornea) which create electrostatic repulsive forces within the stroma. Think of this as an expansive force that is known as the swelling pressure (SP). SP refers to the pressure needed in-vitro to inflate the cornea with a cannula and artificially induce edema and swelling. So a high SP does not mean that the cornea is swollen. Instead, a high SP means that the cornea is resistant to swelling because it has formidable cohesiveness and tensile stiffness (elasticity) that resists expansion. This has been measured around +55 mm Hg. If the stroma is compressed (eg, high IOP, mechanical applanation), then the SP will increase as well. However, if the stroma is expanded (eg, corneal edema), then SP will decrease. The major forces that influence the flow of aqueous into and out of the cornea can be summarized by IP = IOP - SP (where IP is imbibition pressure, IOP is intraocular pressure, and SP is swelling pressure). IP is basically a measurement of the propensity of the cornea to develop edema. As a basic rule, we want IP to be low and ideally negative, because if the IP value increases, then there is likely corneal edema. In vitro, IP = SP (because there's no IOP present, duh!). In vivo, SP is higher than IOP due to the reasons mentioned in the previous paragraph. So usually, IP = IOP - SP ==> 15mm Hg - 55 mm Hg = -40 mg Hg. When IP is negative, then there is no net flow of aqueous into the cornea. However, in pathological states, IP may become positive (ie, either IOP can increase or SP can decrease) and aqueous will enter the cornea edema will ensue. Disruptions to the endothelium (eg, Fuchs) will compromise the integrity of the stroma and will lower the SP value --> increase in IP --> edema. For the sake of completeness, conditions that elevate the IOP (eg, angle closure glaucoma) will then increase the IP as well. Lowering the IOP with topical medications (Choice C) in patients with compromised endothelium can then subsequently reduce the IP. It is noteworthy that the mechanism for hypertonic sodium chloride (Muro 128) is different in that it helps to increase SP which leads to reduced IP. Hence, using both of these medications in synergy may be especially helpful for medical management of corneal edema. While a full review of Fuch's endothelial dystrophy may be found in the explanations to other questions on this website, suffice it to say that vision in these patients is worse in the morning (choice A) and guttae appear centrally at first (choice B). explanation: Avellino corneal dystrophy (ACD) has been reclassified as Granular corneal dystrophy type 2 (GCD2). It can be thought of as a combination of lattice and granular corneal dystrophies. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and is due to a defect in the 5q31 locus (not 7q31) which contains the TGFB1 gene (which itself encodes the keratoepithelin protein). The corneal opacities are described as looking like: stellate (star-like), snowflake, and icicle (see photo). Lattice lines are seen deep to these. Because the deposits in ACD have both lattice and granular-type components, these deposits stain with both Congo Red and Masson Trichrome. The granular-like deposits have a snowflake- like appearance and are located in the anterior to mid-stroma. The lattice lines are located in the deeper stroma. LASIK and LASEK are contraindicated with Avellino dystrophy because they can make the haze worse. Epi-LASIK involves using a blunt microkeratome to remove only the epithelium and then ablating the stromal bed. The plane of separation is between the basement membrane and Bowman's layer. Early reports recommended replacing the cleaved epithelium, but most clinicians abandoned this practice as a benefit was not shown. LASEK involves placing alcohol on the epithelium and then removing the epithelium, lasering the bed, and then placing the epithelium back on the bed. Again, most clinicians have abandoned puting the epithelium back on as a benefit has not been shown. In LASEK, the epithelial basement membrane is cleaved in half between the lamina lucida and lamina densa. Some studies suggested that leaving behind the lamina densa actually gave an improved post-operative refractive result compared to epi-LASIK. These studies combined with a $40,000 price tag for the keratome was a death sentence for the epi-LASIK procedure. PRK (photorefractive keratectomy) involves scraping the epithelium off with a brush or spatula and then ablating the stromal bed.

question: Which of the following is a TRUE statement regarding chemical injuries?

explanation: Actually, acidic chemicals denature and precipitate proteins in the tissues they contact. These precipitated proteins then serve as a type of barrier to further damage by the acidic chemical. In addition, ocular tissues have a higher buffering capacity for acidic compounds. In contrast, alkali chemicals cause saponification of fatty acids in cell membranes (e.g. corneal epithelium) which leads to cellular disruption. After the corneal epithelium is destroyed, the alkali chemical can easily penetrate and destroy the collagen fibrils and proteoglycans in the corneal stroma. In addition, very strong alkali chemicals can eat through the cornea and enter the anterior chamber with disastrous results, including a high incidence of severe glaucoma. The most important step for chemical injuries of any kind is immediate and copious irrigation with water or balanced saline solution. Do NOT try to neutralize a base with an acid or vice versa.

explanation: This is a picture of band keratopathy, a corneal degeneration wherein calcium is deposited into subepithelial layers (primarily epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer and anterior stroma). Deposits may initially be relatively translucent (non light- blocking), but may progress into opaque (light-blocking) entities that may then cause elevations in the overlying epithelial surface, leading to chronic irritation and epitheliopathy. The causes of band keratopathy are many, and can be divided into "C" categories to help make it easier to remember: 1) Chronic eye disease: uveitis, long-standing retinal detachment, late sequelae of HSV infection, chronic corneal graft rejection, phthisis, exposure keratopathy, etc. 2) Causes of increased calcium levels [choice B] (eg, sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, etc). Note there is conflicting evidence in the literature regarding low or high phosphate levels contributing to band keratopathy. 3) Chemical exposure: intraocular silicone oil (choice A), thiazides, mercury, phosphate- containing drops (eg, prednisolone phosphate [not the more commonly used prednisolone acetate]) 4) Congenital causes: congenital eye diseases, such as congenital band keratopathy, Norrie's disease, etc. For mild cases of band keratopathy, treatment primarily involves lubrication of the ocular surface and other comfort measures such as a bandage contact lens. If there are treatable systemic causes of elevated calcium, these should be treated as well and may require co-management with an internist, nephrologist, etc. For advanced, symptomatic cases of band keratopathy, surgical intervention may be required. This includes: a) Manual epithelial debridement (superficial keratectomy) and removal of calcium deposits, with or without 2-5% EDTA (*) as a chelating agent, and with or without diamond-burr polishing of underlying Bowman's membrane. b) Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK): PTK is generally not recommended because the calcium will ablate at a slower rate than the corneal stroma and the patient will wind up with irregular astigmatism. Under desperate circumstances, PTK can be tried after all other therapies have failed. *Clinically relevant note: This may sound obvious, but if you perform a chelation, you must make sure that you do not simply order "EDTA" because the pharmacy may send you CALCIUM EDTA (a more readily available substance), which would be completely useless to remove calcium! You must make sure to order either sodium EDTA or potassium EDTA. Extra: Disease Band Keratopathy is a corneal degeneration that is most often composed of fine dust-like calcium deposits in the sub-epithelium, Bowman’s layer and the anterior stroma. It is typically a band-shaped, horizontal opacity that grows from the peripheral cornea towards the central cornea. Initial deposits are gray but as the deposition progresses, the band becomes chalky- white and with dots in areas of corneal nerves. Band keratopathy can be caused by systemic causes (autoimmune, renal disease), as a result of introacular surgery or chronic intraocular conditions, or be idiopathic. Physical examination Physical exam findings in band keratopathy includes decreased visual acuity (often mild) with characteristic slit lamp exam findings: • Gray-white plaque with fine, dusty deposits in a horizontal band distribution on the cornea • Sparing of the extreme periphery of the cornea (normal lucency) • Lucent holes in plaque (representing corneal nerves through Bowman’s membrane) • Flakey, peripheral plaque.

question: Which of the following conditions can cause the corneal finding seen in the photo above?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts the classic appearance of band keratopathy. There is deposition of calcium mainly in Bowman layer but also some in the anterior stroma. Common causes of band keratopathy include: uveitis, elevated phosphorous level (e.g. in renal failure patients), elevated calcium level (e.g. sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism), and decreased potassium level can predispose to this condition. Also, silicone oil instillation (especially in an aphakic eye) commonly can cause band keratopathy. An unusual cause of band keratopathy is exposure to Mercurial vapors. These calcium deposits can be removed by: (1) First, removing the corneal epithelium (e.g. with alcohol); (2) Applying disodium EDTA to loosen the calcium deposits; and (3) gently removing the deposits by rubbing with Weck-Cel sponges. Some astute OQ users have noted that primary hyperparathyroidism has high calcium levels and low phosphorous levels. Therefore, they believe that answer choice B could be correct. However, it is not the low level of phosphate that is associated with band keratopathy as the question asks. It is the high level of calcium associated with hyperparathyroidism that causes band keratopathy.

question: In addition to calcium, what other substance may deposit in the anterior cornea to cause clinical signs and symptoms of band keratopathy?
explanation: Band keratopathy occurs in "calcific" and "noncalcific" forms. Either entity is caused by a deposition of substances at the level of Bowman's layer. Classic "calcific" band keratopathy refers to the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite and has a multitude of causes including: • Hypercalcemia (e.g. hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity, milk- alkali syndrome). • Chronic ocular disease (e.g. juvenile idiopathic arthritis, interstitial keratitis, phthisis bulbi). • Primary hereditary band keratopathy. • Hyper- and hypo- phosphatasia (e.g. in chronic renal failure patients). • Chronic exposure to mercurial vapors or mercurial preservatives (e.g. in some eyedrops). • silicone oil in aphakic eye. In addition to the classic form of calcific band keratopathy, a similar form of band keratopathy may result from the deposition of urates in the cornea. These deposits are usually brown (compared to the gray-white deposits of calcific band keratopathy) and are often secondary to systemic conditions such as gout or hyperuricemia. Another example of non-calcific band keratopathy occurs in advanced forms of spheroidal degeneration. Classic calcific band keratopathy typically beings at the corneal peripheral at the 3 and 9 o'clock meridians. Typically, this early peripheral form is demarcated from the limbus by a clear zone which is thought to be caused by the buffering capacity of the limbal vessels. Calcific band keratopathy typically begins gray in color but later turns chalky white. If a patient presents with band keratopathy of unknown etiology (e.g. no known chronic ocular inflammation), then a systemic workup should be initiated. An example of a workup for possible systemic causes includes: • serum calcium, phosphorus, uric acid • blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine (Cr) • parathyroid hormone • angiotensin-converting enzyme • urinanalysis If an underlying systemic condition (e.g. hypercalcemia) is found, then it should be treated to help limit the magnitude of band keratopathy. However oftentimes, only incomplete regression of the band keratopathy is achieved. For patients with more advanced forms of band keratopathy affecting their vision or causing ocular discomfort (e.g. photophobia, tearing), then superficial keratectomy using EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) can be employed. The typical protocol involves: 1. Topical anesthetic 2. Scrapping off the corneal epithelium (since EDTA cannot penetrate intact epithelium) 3. Soaking the areas of band keratopathy with EDTA (e.g. 1%) with saturated cellulose sponges. 4. Scrapping off the areas of band keratopathy with a blade. 5. Using a diamond burr to polish the corneal surface to ensure that it is smooth. 6. Apply a bandage contact lens (with or without amniotic membrane) to help with epithelial regrowh, prevention of haze, and improve patient comfort. 7. Topical antibiotic and steroid drops. Summary: band keratopathy is typically caused by calcium hydroxyapatite deposits but can also be caused by deposition of urate.

question: A patient presents to your clinic and states that he was struck in the eye two months ago. He went to the emergency room and they told him that he had a lot of blood inside of his eye. You examine him and note the following findings (see photo). What is the pattern of clearance from the cornea in this condition?
explanation: This is a picture of corneal blood staining. After blood staining occurs, the cornea will clear from the periphery first, then to the center of the cornea (i.e. centripetally). Corneal blood staining is one of the most feared complications that occurs after hyphema, especially in the setting of rebleeding. Approximately <5% of patients after traumatic hyphema develop rebleeding which occurs most frequently between 2 and 5 days after the initial injury. Of those individuals that rebleed, approximately half of them will develop elevated intraocular pressure which predisposes the eye to corneal blood staining. The mechanism of blood staining is that the red blood cells in the anterior chamber release hemoglobin which penetrates the posterior corneal stroma. The keratocytes then absorb the hemoglobin and convert it into hemosiderin which leads to keratocyte death. The reason that corneal blood staining is important is because it can lead to loss of corneal transparency for years and can lead to the development of amblyopia in young children. question: After how many days does rebleeding generally occur after a traumatic hyphema?
explanation: "Rebleeding" is the major worry after a traumatic hyphema since it can lead to corneal blood staining, poorly-controlled glaucoma, and subsequent optic atrophy. Per the BCSC Cornea, it generally occurs 2 to 5 days after the initial hyphema when the original clot retracts. Per the BCSC Glaucoma, it generally occurs 3-7 days after the initial hyphema.

question: How do you distinguish recurrent erosions secondary to a previous history of trauma versus ones that are caused by anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD)?

explanation: The most common causes of recurrent erosion syndrome is from anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD) and secondary to trauma. To distinguish pottraumatic erosion from dystrophic erosion, the examiner should examine the fellow eye after maximal pupillary dilation. It is much easier to detect subtle ABMD changes after the pupil is dilated since the characteristic fingerprints and whorls can be better seen in retroillumination. If no ABMD changes are found, then the most likely cause of the erosions is from previous trauma. ABMD is the most common corneal dystrophy with approximately 6-18% of the population being affected. It is more frequently detected in individuals over the age of 50 years. The characteristic corneal findings found on slit-lamp exam are: fingerprint lines, dots/microcysts; map lines; and bleb/cobblestone pattern. Approximately 10% of patients with ABMD will experience recurrent erosions. Conversely, approximately 50% of patients with recurrent erosions will have ABMD. It typically has a sporadic inheritance, but some cases may follow an autosomal dominant pattern (with incomplete penetrance).

question: Which of the following would be the first-line treatment for recurrent erosions secondary to anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD)?
explanation: Patients with ABMD (aka "map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy") are predisposed to recurrent erosions due to poor adhesion of the epithelium to the underlying basement membrane. Conservative therapy to prevent recurrent erosions consists of hypertonic saline eyedrops and/or bandage contact lens use. Epithelial debridement is a better treatment for epithelial erosions secondary to basement membrane dystrophy. If these fail to prevent the erosions, then more invasive therapy is indicated such as anterior stromal micropuncture or PTK. Recurrent erosions secondary to shearing injuries (e.g. fingernail to the eye) are more amenable to "anterior stromal micropuncture." This procedure consists of using a specially-designed 25-gauge needle and making many superficial puncture wounds in the involved area. These puncture sites are thought to stimulate adhesion of the epithelium to the basement membrane. Care should be exercised in performing this procedure in the visual axis as this procedure can sometimes lead to scarring.

question: Which of the following is most suggestive of congenital glaucoma in a 1-year-old?
explanation: Congenital glaucoma is associated with photophobia, corneal edema, corneal diameter greater than 12 mm, and horizontal tears in Descemet's membrane. Congenital glaucoma displays the triad of photophobia, tearing, and blepharospasm with bright lights. In addition, horizontal diameters are abnormally increased (normal for newborns: 9.5-10.5 mm). The first gene demonstrated to be involved in congenital glaucoma was CYP1B1 which encodes a protein in the cytochrome P450 enzyme family. Though corneal edema can occur in patients with congenital glaucoma, it is not part of the classic triad. This degeneration can occur from chronic keratitis and some causes include phlyctenulosis, trachoma, and interstitial keratitis. It is more common in middle- age and older women. explanation: The brown pigmentation located centrally in this cornea and indicated by the white arrow represents a type of iron line seen in about 80% of patients with prior radial keratotomy. question: Which of the following medications is absorbed into the blood stream, goes to the aqueous and is then absorbed into the posterior cornea and anterior lens capsule resulting in pigment deposition?
explanation: Chlorpromazine (Thorazine) and thioridazine (Mellaril) are phenothiazines. These medications are absorbed in the blood stream and then make their way to the aqueous. From the aqueous they absorb into the posterior cornea and anterior lens capsule and result in pigment deposition. The incidence of this lens opacity depends on both drug dose and treatment duration. This lens opacity does not disappear even with discontinuing the medication, though it generally is visually insignificant. In the retina, chlorpromazine rarely causes damage. At doses normally used (<800 mg/day) thioridazine rarely causes retinopathy. But thioridazine can result in severe retinopathy with high doses. Initially there is RPE stippling in the posterior pole. question: Which of the following is the LEAST LIKELY to cause toxic ulcerative keratopathy?
explanation: Toxic ulcerative keratopathy is the condition caused by topically applied medications. It is due to impaired epithelial wound healing and manifests as a diffuse punctate keratitis which can lead to a persistent epithelial defect. The most common medications associated with this condition include: medications containing BAK, topical anesthetics, topical NSAIDs, trifluoridine, beta-blockers, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Thus, glaucoma patients presenting with persistent corneal epithelial problems should have their medications evaluated as a potential cause. Benzalkonium chloride (BAK) is a common preservative in topical medications that actually increases the potency of drugs by causing a disruption in corneal epithelial cells. Latanoprost is generally a well-tolerated topical medication. Trifluridine 1% (i.e. Viroptic®) is highly toxic to the epithelium and its extended use can result in neurotrophic ulcers. It should generally be stopped after 14 days. Brimonidine 0.2% (i.e. Alphagan®) can cause a follicular conjunctivitis in a large proportion (~15%) of patients. Lower concentrations (e.g. 0.1%) and the use of a non- BAK preservative (e.g. Purite®) help to lower the incidence of this side effec.

question: Which of the following contribute to the cornea's relative immune isolation?

options.A: presence of blood vessels and lymphatics
options.B: downregulation of transforming growth factor betas

explanation: The cornea is considered to be an "immunologically privileged" site meaning that the responsiveness to foreign antigens is relatively suppressed. The BCSC states that this immune privilege can be attributed to the following factors: • Absence of blood vessels and lymphatics. This impairs the delivery of immune effectors cells and the flow of antigens to the draining lymph nodes. • Expression of immunosuppressive factors (e.g. TGF-beta, neuropeptides such as alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone). • Expression of Fas ligand (CD95) by corneal cells. This increased expression is believed to be instrumental in causing Fas-mediated apoptosis of activated lymphocytes. • In general, there is a downregulation of MHC molecules within the cornea.

question: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome?
explanation: Type I immune reactions Are anaphylactic Or atopic reactions. In these reactions, preformed Ige antibodies bound on mast cell receptors react with the antigen causing degranulation of the mast cell with histamine release. An example of a Type I reaction is allergic conjunctivitis. Type II immune reactions are caused by cytotoxic antibodies. This reaction is where antibodies bind to foreign antigen and activate the complement pathway. An example of a type II reaction is ocular cicatricial pemphigoid. Type III immune reactions are also known as " immune-complex reactions." These reactions result from immune complex deposition in tissues which activate the complement and other effector systems. An example of a Type III reaction is "serum sickness", systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Previously, a copy of the BCSC (prior to 2016) fundamentals had listed Stevens Johnson syndrome as a type III reaction. Type IV immune reaction s are delayed hypersensitivity reactions. These involve recruitment of pre-sensitized immune cells. An example of a type IV reaction is allergic contact dermatitis. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome is now classified ed as a type IV immune reaction. Type V immune reactions are a newer class of hypersensitivity reactions called " stimulatory hypersensitivity." This type of reaction occurs when antibodies are produced with the property of stimulating specific cell targets. The most common example would be Graves’ disease which is characterized by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor.

question: A 26-year-old gentleman is referred to you by his optometrist who noted new corneal infiltrates in the right eye.  Of note, the patient was being treated empirically with neomycin ointment after suffering a small corneal abrasion.  On exam, you note several small peripheral, ring-shaped corneal infiltrates in the inferior cornea of the right eye.   There is no epithelial defect overlying these infiltrates.  What type of hypersensitivity reaction do these infiltrates represent?
explanation: Neomycin is known to cause peripheral corneal infiltrates as a possible side effect. These infiltrates are a type of Wessely immune ring which represents the coalescence of local antibodies to antigens with subsequent complement activation. These immune rings are type 3 hypersensitivity reactions. Other conditions that may cause a Wessely ring include corneal foreign body and contact lens reactions. The classic ocular diseases that represent different hypersensitivity reactions include: • type 1 ("anaphylaxis"): allergic/atopic conjunctivitis • type 2 ("cytotoxic antibodies"): ocular cicatricial pemphigoid • type 3 ("immune-complex reactions"): scleritis • type 4 ("cell-mediated reactions"): contact dermatitis, corneal graft rejection, Stevens-Johnson syndrome. • type 5 ("stimulatory hypersensitivity"): thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis Note: older texts, including older versions of the BCSC have listed Stevens-Johnson Syndrome as type III, but recent papers in the literature have listed SJS as type IV. Given the controversy and recent changes, one would hope SJS classification would not be a good exam question.

question: Which of the following statements regarding vernal keratoconjunctivitis is TRUE?

options.A: the palpebral form has giant follicles
options.B: the palpebral form has Horner-Trantas dots
options.D: mast cell stabilizers are used for immediate relief

explanation: A good way of remembering vernal is to know that "vernal" means "Spring". This is a good way of remembering when vernal conjunctivitis occurs and that it is related to an allergic phenomena. This allergic entity typically occurs in children within the first 2 decades of life during the spring or fall. Classic ocular signs include: (1) giant papillary conjunctivitis; (2) "Horner- Trantas dots" which are jellylike limbal nodules representing degenerated eosinophils; and a (3) "shield ulcer" which is a corneal epithelial defect involving the upper half of the cornea. The palpebral form of vernal has giant papillae. The limbal form of vernal has Horner- Trantas dots. Mast cell stabilizers take at least 2 weeks to reach effect. Extra: Differential diagnosis The main differential diagnosis to be considered is atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC). AKC typically has an older age of onset in the 2nd to 5th decade, as opposed to onset prior to age 10 with VKC. Conjunctival involvement is classically on the upper tarsus in VKC and on the lower tarsus in AKC. Additionally, AKC is typically more chronic in nature and more commonly results in scarring of the cornea and conjunctival cicatrization, whereas VKC is typically more self-limiting.
